description: A nearly six-minute fairytale power ballad from Speak Now, written alone after one dazzling first meeting in New York City. Never a single, it became the album's beloved deep cut — and, a decade later, a viral phenomenon.

pops.text: Swift wrote every song on Speak Now by herself, all 14 standard-edition tracks. 'Enchanted' sits ninth, and she co-produced it with Nathan Chapman.
She wrote it about a man she was infatuated with after meeting him in person in New York City — and spent the song hoping the feeling might continue, and be returned.
The word 'wonderstruck' is a planted clue: the man had used it in an email to Swift after they met, and she deliberately worked it into the lyrics hoping he would notice.
The Speak Now booklet hides a message in capital letters for this song: 'A-D-A-M.' Fans quickly connected it to Adam Young, founder of Owl City.

Young answered in song: on February 13, 2011 he posted his own cover of 'Enchanted,' rewriting lines to reply to hers — 'Taylor, I was so in love with you.' Swift never publicly responded, and never confirmed or denied he was the subject.

This was almost the album's title track. Swift planned to call the album Enchanted until Big Machine president Scott Borchetta argued the word did not fit the record's grown-up perspectives — so it became Speak Now.

Musically it is a slow-build power ballad: gentle acoustic guitar, a crescendo after every 'I was enchanted to meet you,' then electric guitars, steady drums and a harmony-layered coda. Swift called the pleading bridge her favorite part — pure stream of consciousness.
Never released as a single, it still debuted at No. 75 on the Billboard Hot 100 in November 2010 on album buzz alone, and was certified gold in the US in 2014.
The song even became a perfume: Swift's first fragrance, launched in October 2011, was named Wonderstruck after its key word, followed in July 2012 by a second scent, Wonderstruck Enchanted.

In late 2021 the song went viral on TikTok and charted all over again, more than a decade on. On the Eras Tour it was the only Speak Now song performed every night until 'Long Live' joined it on July 7, 2023 — the day Speak Now (Taylor's Version), with the re-recorded 'Enchanted,' was released.

title: Enchanted

description: A bright, increasingly frantic Anastasio–Marshall miniature from the concept album Rift — a gift, a string of pearls, and a singer who ends up laughing and falling apart as the tempo runs away with him.

pops.text: Written by guitarist Trey Anastasio and lyricist Tom Marshall, Phish's longtime songwriting partnership, with Anastasio singing lead.
It is track five on Rift, clocking in at 3:54 — one of the shortest, punchiest songs on an album full of long proggy pieces.
Rift is a concept album: one sleepless night in the life of a man dreaming about the rift in his relationship. 'Sparkle' is one of the dream's stranger rooms.

The album was recorded in September–October 1992 at White Crow Studios in Burlington, Vermont, with additional work in Nashville, produced by Barry Beckett, and released by Elektra on February 2, 1993.
The lyric opens under social pressure: 'The pressure builds, you buy a gift, you're hoping that your dread will lift.' The verses name-check friends — Luce, Lil', Ed and Jill.
Its central image is jewelry as a trap: friends 'confine you in their worlds, one by one, a string of pearls' — until the singer releases the links and undoes the clasp.
Then it turns surreal: 'The skin that drips down from the tree and peels back slowly from your knee erupts into your lung and heart.' Dream logic, Rift-style.
The ending is the joke and the payoff: 'You laugh and laughing, fall apart' repeats and repeats while the band speeds up, bluegrass-fast, until the song collapses in giggles.
David Welker's Rift cover painting is a visual track listing — its dreamlike scene illustrates nearly every song on the album, 'Sparkle' included.
In concert it became one of the most-played songs from Rift, a first-set energy burst for decades, turning up on a string of Live Phish releases including the New Year's Eve 1995 shows.

title: Sparkle

description: Two and a half minutes of jangly alarm clock from Green — Michael Stipe's affectionate wake-up call to a bandmate who loved to sleep in, complete with a bridge full of chiming music boxes.

pops.text: Track two on Green, and the shortest burst on the album at just 2:35 — 'Sleep delays my life,' it begins. Naturally.
Green was R.E.M.'s sixth album and their first for Warner Bros. after the I.R.S. years, released in November 1988. The major-label move made stars of them.
Stipe wrote the lyric as a polite jab at bassist Mike Mills, who kept sleeping late during the Green sessions while Stipe was up early, full of ideas and ready to work.
The best part: Mills did not know the song was about him for nearly a decade — not until a concert in the late 1990s, when Stipe introduced it that way on stage.
Drummer Bill Berry got the last laugh on tape, pointing out that on the recording it is Mills' vocal that enters before Stipe's — proof he beat the singer to the studio that day.
Hear that dreamy clatter in the bridge? Several music boxes playing at once — Berry's idea, which came to him in a dream, for a song that turned out to be about sleep.
The video was made by a young filmmaker fresh out of CalArts' experimental animation program named Eric Darnell — who went on to co-direct the hit animated films Antz and Madagascar.
This upload is the 'Pop Screen Video Version' of Darnell's clip, posted by the band's own remhq channel.

As a single it was the album's quiet ending: fourth and final single from Green, released in the US only in September 1989, it failed to chart on the Hot 100 — unlike 'Stand' and 'Orange Crush' before it.
Stipe rated it higher than the charts did: in the 1989 concert film Tourfilm he introduces 'Get Up' as his favorite song. Green itself went double platinum and reached No. 12 in the US.

title: Get Up

description: The Stones go disco — a slinky, harmonica-and-bass groove born in New York clubland that became their eighth and final US No. 1 single, leading off the Some Girls comeback.

pops.text: It started as a jam: Mick Jagger messing around with keyboardist Billy Preston during rehearsals for the band's March 1977 El Mocambo club gigs in Toronto.
Was it meant to be disco? Jagger and Ronnie Wood insisted not — but Keith Richards countered: ''Miss You' was a damn good disco record; it was calculated to be one.'
Charlie Watts confirmed the club influence: many Some Girls songs 'were heavily influenced by going to the discos — you can hear it in the four-to-the-floor drumming.'

That famous bass line is Bill Wyman's, built from Preston's bass part on the demo. Engineer Chris Kimsey recalled Wyman visiting quite a few clubs before he got the bass line sorted — 'which made that song.'
The wailing harmonica is Sugar Blue, an American blues player who, according to Wood, Jagger discovered busking on the streets of Paris.

Unusually for Some Girls, the track is full of guests: Sugar Blue, Ian McLagan on Wurlitzer electric piano, and Mel Collins playing the tenor sax solo. It was recorded at Pathé-Marconi studios in Paris in late 1977.
Released May 10, 1978, a month ahead of Some Girls, with the tongue-in-cheek country pastiche 'Far Away Eyes' — another album track — as its B-side.
On August 5, 1978 it hit No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, ending the seven-week reign of Andy Gibb's 'Shadow Dancing.' It was the Stones' eighth US No. 1 — and their last. It reached No. 3 in the UK.

The original take ran about nine minutes. It was edited to 4:48 for the album and 3:35 for the single, while an 8:26 'Special Disco Version' — the band's first 12-inch dance remix, by a young Bob Clearmountain — came out on a 12-inch single, some copies on pink vinyl.
Rolling Stone placed it at No. 498 on its 500 Greatest Songs list, and in 2002 Dr. Dre remixed it for the film Austin Powers in Goldmember — disco Stones, sampled by hip-hop.

title: Miss You

description: Widespread Panic's rock-radio breakthrough is a borrowed song — a Bloodkin cover from Athens friends Daniel Hutchens and Eric Carter, given a big, rolling groove on Ain't Life Grand.

pops.text: This is a cover. The song was written by Daniel Hutchens and Eric Carter of Bloodkin, fellow Athens, Georgia songwriters in Panic's inner circle.
Hutchens and Carter met at age eight in Ripley, West Virginia, and by the early 1990s the pair had written more than 300 songs together as Bloodkin.
Panic loved Bloodkin's writing so much they recorded three of their songs for studio albums: 'Makes Sense to Me,' 'Henry Parsons Died' and this one.
Panic first played their version live on July 9, 1993, at a H.O.R.D.E. Festival stop in Forest Lake, Minnesota — before it had a studio home.
It landed on Ain't Life Grand, the band's fourth studio album, released on Capricorn Records on September 6, 1994 — their most accessible record to that point.

Ain't Life Grand hides a secret at the end: an unlisted solo acoustic piece by guitarist Michael Houser with a title as long as a chorus — 'Waiting For The Wind To Blow Down The Tree In My Back Yard.'
Released as a single in 1995, 'Can't Get High' became Widespread Panic's breakthrough on rock radio, carrying the Athens jam band well beyond the Southeast club circuit.
The video here is the song's official music video, posted on the band's own YouTube channel and featured on widespreadpanic.com as the Ain't Life Grand clip.
On April 6, 1995 Panic made their Late Night with Conan O'Brien debut with this song — and the show's house band, the Max Weinberg 7, sat in with their horn section.
Live, it was a staple through 1998, turned into a rarity, then returned to regular rotation in 2003. Since Hutchens' death in May 2021, Panic's performances of his songs carry an extra weight.

title: Can't Get High

description: A 1920s jug-band blues supercharged by a teenage Bob Weir and the brand-new Grateful Dead on their debut album — the first of the song's many lives under ever-longer names.

pops.text: The roots run deep: harmonica player Noah Lewis recorded 'Minglewood Blues' in 1928 with Cannon's Jug Stompers, one of the great Memphis jug bands.
In 1930 Lewis cut a different song under his own name and called it 'New Minglewood Blues.' The Dead covered that one — and, in the spirit of the thing, added a second 'New.'
Bob Weir brought the song to the band, added a verse of his own, and sings lead — he was just 19 years old when the debut album was made.
Minglewood itself is real: Mengelwood, Tennessee, a company town built around the Mengel Box Company, whose wooden-box works employed the song's drifters.
The debut album was a rush job: recorded in just four days at RCA's Studio A in Los Angeles with producer David Hassinger, and released March 17, 1967.
On the original LP the track was edited down to 2:31. The version in this video is the full-length 2:40 cut, restored when the album was reissued in 2003.
Authorship was muddy at first: the song was originally listed as a band composition under the Dead's collective pseudonym 'McGannahan Skjellyfetti,' before later editions credited Noah Lewis.
Listen for Ron 'Pigpen' McKernan pumping the Vox Continental organ — the garage-band engine of the 1967 Dead, next to Garcia's cutting lead guitar.
This early arrangement left the repertoire after 1971 and stayed shelved for about five years, until the band revived the song in 1976 with mostly new lyrics.
Reborn as 'All New Minglewood Blues' on 1978's Shakedown Street, it settled into the name 'New Minglewood Blues' and became a swaggering first-set staple for the rest of the Dead's career.

title: New New Minglewood Blues

description: Paul McCartney's car-ride consolation for a five-year-old Julian Lennon grew into a seven-minute anthem — the first Apple single, a nine-week US No. 1, and the most famous singalong coda in rock.

pops.text: In June 1968 McCartney drove out to Weybridge to check on Cynthia Lennon and her five-year-old son Julian, whose parents had just split. He composed the song in the car on the way.
It began as 'Hey Jules' — for Julian. McCartney changed Jules to Jude simply 'because I thought that sounded a bit better.'
Paul planned to fix the line 'the movement you need is on your shoulder,' calling it a stupid expression. John Lennon stopped him: 'You won't, you know. That's the best line in the song.' It stayed.
Lennon later heard the song differently — as a message to himself. In 1980 he said Paul was subconsciously giving him his blessing to leave Cynthia for Yoko Ono: 'Go out and get her.'
After 25 rehearsal takes at EMI, the master was cut at Trident Studios to use its eight-track machine — 'Hey Jude' was the first Beatles song recorded on eight-track equipment.
McCartney started the master take not realising Ringo Starr had slipped out for a toilet break. Ringo tiptoed back past his back mid-take — and hit his drum cue perfectly.

A 36-piece orchestra was overdubbed onto the coda, then asked to clap and sing along for double pay. All but one agreed; the holdout declared, 'I'm not going to clap my hands and sing Paul McCartney's bloody song!'
The 'na-na-na' coda runs for over four minutes of the song's 7:11 — an audacious length that made 'Hey Jude' the longest single ever to top the British charts at the time.

Released August 26, 1968 as the first single on the Beatles' own Apple label, backed with 'Revolution,' it spent nine weeks at No. 1 in the US — tying the all-time record — and sold an estimated eight million copies.

The promo film, shot at Twickenham by Michael Lindsay-Hogg and aired on David Frost's Frost on Sunday, ends with some 300 audience members joining the coda around the band. Ringo had quit the group days earlier and returned just in time to film it. This is the 2015 remaster.

title: Hey Jude

description: The somber heart of Rosemary, the Chapel Hill band's debut — a jangly, harmony-rich elegy for a 'stepchild' failed by every adult around him, and a signature song of the 1990s North Carolina college-rock scene.

pops.text: Track four on Rosemary, running 3:07 — the darkest song on a debut album otherwise full of sunny, jangly guitar pop.

Dillon Fence formed in 1986 at the University of North Carolina in Chapel Hill, originally under the name the Magoos. Singer-guitarist Greg Humphreys and bassist Chris Goode had played together since high school.
The band's name comes from a regionally famous landmark: an elaborate folk-art fence in Dillon, South Carolina, that members came across around their first shows under the new name.
Carrboro-based Mammoth Records signed them in 1991 and issued a 'Christmas' CD-single that year; the debut album Rosemary followed in 1992.
Rosemary was produced by Ron Saint Germain, and it made Dillon Fence one of the biggest draws on the Southeastern college circuit.
The classic lineup: Greg Humphreys on guitar and lead vocals — the band's songwriter — Kent Alphin on guitar, Chris Goode on bass, and Scott Carle on drums.
The lyric is a search: the narrator runs to the park and down to the beach after dark, looking for the boy he calls 'stepchild,' and lands on the chorus's bleak summary — 'the hate you inherited.'
Its plea is the album's most quoted line: 'You deserve the wealth of a word.' The verses indict the adults — including a cruel teacher of whom Humphreys sings, 'Teacher doesn't know your name.'
The song kept resurfacing: an acoustic version appeared on the band's Daylight EP, and the album version was chosen for the 2004 career compilation Best +.

The band split in 1995 after Mammoth rejected demos for a fourth album, but regrouped in December 2000 to record the double live album Live at the Cat's Cradle — and 'Sad Inheritance' remains in their reunion setlists, through the Rosemary 35th-anniversary shows.

title: Sad Inheritance
Part of Your World
description: Ariel perches in her secret grotto, surrounded by salvaged human treasures, and sings Disney's defining 'I Want' song — a mermaid's daydream of walking, dancing and asking questions on land.

pops.text: This was the first song Howard Ashman and Alan Menken wrote for The Little Mermaid, back in 1986 — before Menken had even officially signed on as composer.
Ashman called it Ariel's 'I Want' song: not a love song about Prince Eric, but a song about her fascination with the whole human world, which he felt the story needed more.
The songwriters jokingly nicknamed it 'Somewhere That's Wet' — they saw it as an underwater cousin of 'Somewhere That's Green' from their musical Little Shop of Horrors.
Jodi Benson had worked with Ashman on the stage musical Smile. He sent the whole female cast of Smile the song to audition with — without telling them what the project was.
Benson's audition was an anonymous reel-to-reel tape mailed to Disney. The directors picked her tape without knowing whose it was, and she learned she had the part about a year later.
Ashman coached Benson from inside the recording booth, whispering direction as she sang — and some of his breathing can reportedly still be heard on the finished track.
Benson asked for the studio lights to be dimmed so she could feel like she was deep underwater, and Ashman urged her to treat the song like a spoken monologue rather than belting it.
Menken and Ashman deliberately kept takes that were not perfectly sung — spoken bits and plain, unpolished notes — because they wanted Ariel to sound real, not like a concert singer.

Animator Glen Keane asked to animate Ariel after hearing Benson sing this song, and he animated the whole sequence himself — including a tricky shot that seems to circle around her in the grotto, drawn without computer help.

Disney executive Jeffrey Katzenberg wanted the song cut after restless kids at an early test screening — one spilled his popcorn. Ashman fought for it, a later screening in colour won the room, and Katzenberg later admitted he was embarrassed he had ever wanted it gone.

title: Shiny
description: Giant treasure-hoarding crab Tamatoa drapes himself in gold and glow in his lair beneath the sea, belting a glam-rock villain song while Moana and Maui try not to become dinner.

pops.text: Tamatoa is a giant coconut crab who lives in Lalotai, the realm of monsters, and has covered his shell with treasure he has collected from the ocean floor.
The song was written by Lin-Manuel Miranda, with music by Miranda and Mark Mancina, for Disney's Moana — Miranda's first film songwriting job, landed while Hamilton was taking off.
Miranda has said 'Shiny' was partly a tribute to David Bowie: he had been listening to Bowie on a loop after Bowie's death in January 2016 while writing it.

The Bowie link runs deeper — Jemaine Clement's comedy duo Flight of the Conchords had performed a famous Bowie tribute at the Aspen Comedy Festival in 2004, which helped inspire Miranda once Clement was cast.
Clement, best known from Flight of the Conchords and What We Do in the Shadows, voices Tamatoa as well as singing — giving the crab a sly, preening, show-off delivery.
In the film the number flips into a glowing, black-light style sequence as Tamatoa tries to dazzle — and eat — his guests, a visual feint that lets Maui attempt an escape.
Tamatoa brags that being shiny keeps him safe: predators leave the glittering crab alone, so his vanity doubles as armour in the lyric's logic.
The track runs just over three minutes on the Moana soundtrack album, released by Walt Disney Records in November 2016, a few days before the film opened.
Unlike Moana's voyage songs, which draw on Samoan, Tokelauan and Tuvaluan lyrics by Opetaia Foa'i, 'Shiny' is a pure English-language glam showpiece — the soundtrack's deliberate odd one out.
The official DisneyMusicVEVO film clip has become one of Moana's most rewatched musical moments, keeping Tamatoa — who only appears for this one big scene — among the film's most quoted characters.

title: Move on Up
description: Horns blazing and congas racing under Curtis Mayfield's gentle high tenor — a nearly nine-minute surge of encouragement from his solo debut that simply refuses to sit down.

pops.text: This is the extended album version from Curtis, Mayfield's solo debut, released in September 1970 on his own label, Curtom Records, which he had founded in 1968.
Mayfield had just left the Impressions, the group he led through civil-rights-era classics like 'People Get Ready' and 'Keep On Pushing,' to go solo.
The album version runs nearly nine minutes and even includes a false ending — the groove seems to finish, then surges back in for another lap.
Listen for the racing percussion: conga player Henry Gibson — known as Master Henry Gibson — drives the track's fast, rolling pulse.
It was recorded in 1970 at RCA Studios in Chicago, Mayfield's hometown, and produced by Mayfield himself.
As a US single in 1971 it failed to chart at all — hard to believe given how famous it became later.
Britain got it: an edited version spent 10 weeks in the UK top 50 in 1971 and peaked at number 12.
Disco trio Destination folded 'Move On Up' into a 1979 medley with Mayfield's 'Keep On Pushing' and took it to number one on the US disco chart for four weeks.
Producer Just Blaze slowed down this song's horns to build Kanye West's 2006 single 'Touch the Sky' — one of hip-hop's best-known Mayfield samples.

Rolling Stone placed it at No. 474 on its 2021 list of the 500 Greatest Songs of All Time, and it has since become a post-match anthem for Arsenal fans at the Emirates Stadium and a walkout song in Joe Biden's 2020 campaign.

description: Born from loss: after a fire damaged his home, Robert Smith found singed photographs of his wife Mary in the remains — and turned them into this sweeping, lovelorn highlight of Disintegration. This entry uses the official Tim Pope music video on TheCureVEVO — the shorter single edit — not the full seven-and-a-half-minute album version.

pops.text: You're watching the official music video, which uses the shorter single edit of the song. On the album Disintegration, 'Pictures of You' runs a full 7:29 — the single version trims it down to a remix edit of about 4:46.

The song's spark was a house fire. Going through the remains of his home, Robert Smith came across his wallet holding pictures of his wife, Mary — and one of those very photos became the cover of this single.
That same photo of Mary had already appeared once before in Cure history: it was also used, heavily warped and distorted, as the cover of the earlier single 'Charlotte Sometimes.'

It's the second track on Disintegration, the Cure's eighth studio album, released on Fiction Records on 2 May 1989. The album became the band's commercial peak, reaching No. 3 in the UK and No. 12 in the US.

Director Tim Pope shot this video with three Super-8 cameras at the foot of Buachaille Etive Mòr in Glencoe, Scotland, in February 1990 — during the 'week of the big snow.' Smith later said he had never been colder.

The song is written in the key of A major. Smith sings and plays six-string bass and keyboards on it — while bandmate Lol Tolhurst is credited with 'other instruments' even though he doesn't actually play on this track.

It was released on 19 March 1990 as the fourth and final single from Disintegration — nearly a year after the album itself. Even so, it still climbed to No. 24 on the UK Singles Chart, No. 9 in Ireland and No. 71 on the US Billboard Hot 100.

Remix collectors had a field day: two different UK 12-inch singles carried two different remixes. One, the 'Strange mix,' later turned up on the remix album Mixed Up as the Extended Dub Mix, rebuilt with wholly original drum and bass parts.
The single's other tracks were live recordings from Wembley in July 1989 — 'Last Dance,' 'Fascination Street,' 'Prayers for Rain' and 'Disintegration' — capturing the band on the Disintegration tour.

Its reputation keeps growing: Rolling Stone placed it at No. 283 on its 500 Greatest Songs of All Time, Billboard ranked it No. 9 among the Cure's 40 greatest songs, and Mojo put it at No. 11 of their 30. It has since been certified Silver in the UK and Gold in New Zealand.

title: Pictures of You
Drown
description: A hazy, slow-building daydream of guitars that drifts for minutes, then dissolves into waves of feedback — the Pumpkins' contribution to Cameron Crowe's Seattle-scene film Singles.

pops.text: Billy Corgan wrote 'Drown' shortly after the Pumpkins' debut album Gish came out, and the band first played it live while touring that record.
It was written fresh for Cameron Crowe's 1992 film Singles — not a leftover — and it closes the film's soundtrack album as its final track.

The Singles soundtrack was a snapshot of the Seattle grunge moment, with Pearl Jam, Alice in Chains and Soundgarden alongside Chicago's Pumpkins; it peaked at number 6 on the Billboard 200 and went double platinum in the US.
The very first take of 'Drown' was recorded at Waterfront Studios in New York, a studio owned by Lenny Kravitz, who was then a labelmate on Virgin Records.
Corgan produced the song with Butch Vig, the producer behind Gish — and behind Nirvana's Nevermind the year before.
On the soundtrack the song runs over eight minutes; radio mostly played only the first, song-shaped half, steering clear of the long feedback ending.
It was issued only as a promotional single, never sold in shops — yet it still became the band's highest-charting single at the time, reaching number 24 on Billboard's Alternative Songs chart.
That sprawling ending is built on feedback and an E-Bow, a handheld device that makes guitar strings sing and sustain without picking.

When the band's greatest-hits album Rotten Apples arrived in 2001, 'Drown' was trimmed from over eight minutes to about four and a half, cutting the feedback coda — that edited version is the one on the official audio upload used here.

An early demo of 'Drown,' running close to nine minutes, was later given away through the band's Smashing Pumpkins Record Club archive project, alongside demos of future Siamese Dream songs like 'Luna.'

title: My Sweet Lord
description: George Harrison's gentle prayer builds from acoustic guitar into Phil Spector's Wall of Sound, its 'hallelujah' choruses slowly turning into 'Hare Krishna' — and the official video, made 50 years later, sends two agents searching for something unseen.

pops.text: Harrison began writing the song in December 1969 in Copenhagen, while touring with Delaney & Bonnie — slipping away from a backstage press conference to vamp chords upstairs, alternating 'hallelujah' and 'Hare Krishna.'
He took his melodic inspiration, he later said, from the Edwin Hawkins Singers' version of the old hymn 'Oh Happy Day.'
Harrison first gave the song away: Billy Preston recorded it first, with Harrison co-producing, for Preston's album Encouraging Words, released in September 1970.
Harrison's own version was recorded at Abbey Road Studios in London with Phil Spector co-producing; Ringo Starr, Eric Clapton and members of Badfinger are among the musicians on the session.
The recording helped introduce Harrison's signature slide-guitar sound — one biographer called it as distinctive a signature as the mark of Zorro.

Released as his first solo single in November 1970, it topped charts worldwide, was the biggest-selling single of 1971 in the UK, and became the first number-one single by any ex-Beatle in both the US and Britain.

Midway through, the backing chant switches from 'hallelujah' to the Hare Krishna mantra — Harrison said he wanted listeners chanting it before they knew what was happening, and to show the two phrases meant much the same thing.

Its success brought a famous lawsuit: in 1976 a US court ruled Harrison had subconsciously plagiarised the Chiffons' 1963 hit 'He's So Fine.' He responded, in part, by writing the wry song 'This Song' about the case.
Harrison reworked it as 'My Sweet Lord (2000)' for the 30th-anniversary reissue of All Things Must Pass, and after his death in 2001 the original reached number one in the UK again in January 2002.

This official video arrived in December 2021, over 50 years after the song: directed by Lance Bangs, it stars Fred Armisen and Vanessa Bayer as metaphysical agents working for Mark Hamill, with more than 40 cameos including Ringo Starr.

title: Duke of Earl
description: 'Du-du-du-Duke of Earl' — a doo-wop chant turned royal promise, with Chandler serenading his future duchess over rolling harmonies in one of the most recognisable openings in pop.

pops.text: It began as a warm-up: Chicago vocal group the Dukays would loosen up by singing 'do do do' in different keys before shows.
One day lead singer Eugene Dixon playfully worked baritone Earl Edwards's name into the chant — and 'du-du-du-Duke of Earl' stuck.
Dixon, Edwards and the group's mentor Bernice Williams shaped the chant into a full song, and all three share the writing credit.
The Dukays recorded it, but their label preferred another song, 'Nite Owl,' and let 'Duke of Earl' go to the bigger Vee-Jay label instead.
Because the Dukays' name was tied to their old label, the record came out as a solo single — and Eugene Dixon needed a new stage name.
He built one from his favourite actor, Jeff Chandler: Eugene Dixon became Gene Chandler, and 'Duke of Earl' was his debut under that name.
Released in late 1961, the single entered the Billboard Hot 100 in January 1962 and spent three weeks at number one on both the pop and R&B charts.
Chandler leaned all the way into the part, dubbing himself 'the Duke of Earl' and performing in tails with a cane, monocle, top hat and cape.
The territory he promises his duchess in the lyric is a 'dukedom' — not the technically correct 'duchy' — a word choice generations of fans have happily sung along with anyway.
In 2002 the song was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame, and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame also named it one of its 500 Songs that Shaped Rock and Roll.
